hints: Remember what each part of a Boltzmann curve represents, the shape of the curve versus the position of the activation energy mark.
Think about what a catalyst actually does, it provides a different reaction pathway but does it change the energy of the particles themselves?
Since temperature is unchanged, ask yourself whether the distribution can shift, and what must happen to the X line to give more successful collisions.
walkthrough:
**Recall what the diagram shows**

Think of the curve as a snapshot of how energy is shared out between particles at a given temperature.

The area under the curve to the right of $X$ represents particles with $E \ge E_a$ that can react on collision.

**Recall what a catalyst does**

A catalyst speeds up a reaction by providing an alternative route with a lower activation energy.

It is not used up, and it does not change the starting reactants or products:
$$E_{a}(catalysed) < E_{a}(uncatalysed)$$

**Apply same temperature condition**

At the same temperature, the average energy and the spread of energies do not change.

So the shape and position of the Boltzmann distribution curve stays exactly the same, only the $X$ marker moves to a lower energy value, giving a larger area beyond $E_a$.

options.A: Incorrect. Particle energies depend on temperature, not on catalyst. More particles with higher $E$ would require heating, which shifts the whole distribution to the right. A catalyst at the same temperature leaves particle energies unchanged.
options.B: Incorrect. The peak (most probable energy) moves left only if temperature is lowered. The question states temperature is the same, so the distribution, including the peak, does not move. This confuses the effect of cooling with the effect of a catalyst.
options.C: Incorrect. The peak moves right and flattens only if temperature is increased. A catalyst does not give particles more energy, it just gives them an easier route to react. This confuses the effect of heating with the effect of a catalyst.
options.D: Correct. An effective catalyst provides an alternative mechanism with lower activation energy. On the diagram the curve is unchanged (same $T$) but the $X$ line shifts left to a lower $E$ value, so many more particles now have $E \ge E_a$.
